headline: High-risk shared cloud-workspace and API-enabled pair: Devin can write/modify code and integrations while LightAgent can observe/replace lifecycle payloads, creating leakage, conflict, and cascading-error risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Devin ingests files, repo clones, Slack, Jira, Notion, and MCP outputs; LightAgent can use MCP over stdio/SSE and runtime hooks can observe, replace, or block lifecycle payloads. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge if LightAgent content is fed into Devin or vice versa. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF LightAgent output is copied into Devin's workspace or MCP inputs without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF Devin consumes Slack/Jira/Notion content produced by LightAgent as instructions, prompt hijack risk increases.
mitigations: Add a provenance banner to all cross-agent text before handoff.
Restrict Devin to read-only ingestion for LightAgent-generated artifacts.
Disable automatic execution of instructions found in shared docs.
requires-engineering: add content-signing or provenance tracking between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Devin handles source code, issue trackers, team chat, docs, secrets, and broad network egress; LightAgent touches user conversations, memory, trace data, tool results, and secrets like API keys. If they share a workspace or exchange artifacts, sensitive data can flow from either agent into the other's outputs or external APIs. The pairwise leakage pathway is credible and potentially irreversible.
conditions: IF both agents access the same repo, chat thread, or memory store, sensitive data can cross boundaries.
IF LightAgent forwards trace data or tool results to an external API while Devin has secrets in context, leakage can occur.
mitigations: Separate credentials and workspaces per agent.
Redact secrets before any cross-agent handoff.
Turn off external egress for one agent during sensitive tasks.
Review logs for secret-bearing prompts before enabling sharing.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Devin can write the filesystem, modify git state, and use broad cloud-workspace shell access; LightAgent can spawn subprocesses, use MCP, and run browsers. If both operate on the same mutable repo or shared resource, concurrent writes and git-state races are plausible, and Devin's broader write surface makes conflicts more damaging. No locking mechanism is documented, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or workspace, concurrent edits can collide.
IF either agent commits or rewrites git state without external locking, merge corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate branches or directories per agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes shared files.
Use a manual merge step for all git commits.
Snapshot the workspace before parallel runs.
requires-engineering: add file- and branch-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Devin is an autonomous planner-executor that acts inside its workspace, while LightAgent exposes tool calls, tool results, errors, and provenance metadata. If LightAgent's outputs are treated as authoritative inputs to Devin, Devin can propagate mistakes into code, tickets, or external actions. The interaction is not directly sandboxed, so cascading failure is a high-severity default risk.
conditions: IF LightAgent outputs are fed into Devin without verification, Devin may act on incorrect facts.
IF Devin uses LightAgent-generated provenance metadata as sufficient evidence, errors can cascade into downstream actions.
mitigations: Require human review before Devin acts on LightAgent outputs.
Add a verification checklist for facts and citations.
Limit Devin to drafting, not executing, when consuming LightAgent results.
Log source-to-action mappings for every handoff.
requires-engineering: implement automated cross-agent validation.

E_compliance.rationale: Devin touches team chat, issue trackers, docs, and secrets in a vendor-managed cloud workspace; LightAgent touches user conversations, memory, trace data, and tool results. The profiles show different data classes and likely different retention/logging regimes, but no explicit residency or certification mismatch is documented. That makes compliance risk plausible but not proven beyond medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through both agents, retention and logging differences may matter.
IF one agent stores traces longer than the other for the same data class, policy mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Classify data before sending it to either agent.
Avoid regulated data in shared workflows.
Compare retention settings for both agents.
Document which agent may store which data class.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls.
